title: Missing Number
description:
# Missing Number

Given an integer array `nums` of length `n`, the array contains `n` distinct values chosen from the inclusive range `[0, n]`. Exactly one value from that range is absent. Return the missing value.

The length of the array defines the upper endpoint of the range. For example, if `nums.length == 3`, the complete candidate set is `{0, 1, 2, 3}`, not only the valid array indices.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [3,0,1]
**Output:** 2
**Explanation:** The full range is `[0,3]`. Values 0, 1, and 3 are present, so 2 is missing.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [0,1]
**Output:** 2
**Explanation:** The full range is `[0,2]`. The missing value may be the upper endpoint `n`.

## Example 3:

**Input:** nums = [9,6,4,2,3,5,7,0,1]
**Output:** 8
**Explanation:** The full range is `[0,9]`, and 8 is the only value that does not appear.

## Constraints:

*   `n == nums.length`
*   `1 <= n <= 10^4`
*   `0 <= nums[i] <= n`
*   All values in `nums` are unique.

solutions.name: XOR Index and Value Cancellation
solutions.description:
## Approach

Start an XOR accumulator with `n`, then XOR every array index and every value stored at that index. Every value that is present in the array cancels with the same value from the complete range.

## Key Insight

The complete range is `0..n`, while the valid indices are only `0..n-1`. Initializing with `n` includes the one endpoint that does not have an array index. XOR is also immune to arithmetic overflow.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Gauss Sum with Long Accumulator
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compute the expected sum of the complete range `0..n`, subtract the sum of the values that actually appear in the array, and return the difference.

## Key Insight

The mathematical formula is short, but the multiplication should be promoted before it happens. Using `long expected = (long) n * (n + 1) / 2` keeps the teaching solution correct even when future constraints grow.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Sorting Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort the array, then compare each position `i` with `nums[i]`. The first mismatch is the missing number; if every index matches, the missing value is `n`.

## Key Insight

After sorting, the problem becomes a direct comparison between the ordered values and their natural indices. This is slower than XOR or summation, but it is the most visual baseline for understanding the range invariant.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(log n)

solutions.name: Boolean Seen Table
solutions.description:
## Approach

Allocate a boolean table of size `n + 1`, mark every value that appears in `nums`, then scan the table from 0 to n and return the first unmarked value.

## Key Insight

This route trades memory for directness. It is the clearest hash-table-style formulation and makes both endpoint cases explicit because the table has a slot for `n` as well as for every array index.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: In-Place Cyclic Placement
solutions.description:
## Approach

Repeatedly move any value smaller than `n` into the index equal to that value. The value `n` has no matching index, so leave it wherever it is. After placement, the first index whose value differs from the index is missing.

## Key Insight

The array itself can serve as the lookup table because every legal value except `n` maps to one valid index. Each successful swap places at least one value into its final slot, so the loop remains linear.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)
